ch01.note: The Japanese took Hong Kong on 25 December 1941 (“Black Christmas”) and interned Allied nationals there — British and other Allied civilians at Stanley Camp, captured servicemen at camps such as Sham Shui Po. The English surgeon is such a prisoner, brought under guard to consult on the wound. Historically grounded.

No. 76 Jessfield Road (today Wanhangdu Road) was the headquarters of the secret service of Wang Jingwei’s collaborationist government, established under Japanese direction by the turncoats Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun and moved there in the spring of 1939. Its formal name — the gilt title on the false credential just described — was the Secret Service Headquarters of the Special Affairs Committee of the collaborationist Kuomintang’s Central Executive Committee. It became a byword for torture and murder. Historical.

Wang Jingwei (1883–1944), once a leading figure of the Nationalist party and heir to Sun Yat-sen’s mantle, broke with Chongqing and in March 1940 set up a Japanese-sponsored “reorganized” National Government at Nanjing. Most Chinese regarded it as a puppet regime of collaborators — the 汪伪, the “Wang puppet” apparatus that runs through these stories. Historical.

Ding Mocun (1901–1947) is a real figure: a Nationalist intelligence officer who defected and, with Li Shiqun, ran the No. 76 secret service of the Wang Jingwei regime, later holding ministerial posts under it. He was tried as a traitor and shot in 1947. Historical.

A real event, lightly fictionalized. On 21 December 1939 Ding Mocun escaped an assassination attempt at the Siberia Fur Store, at the corner of Bubbling Well Road and Gordon Road in Shanghai, when his mistress Zheng Pingru led him into an ambush; the episode is the historical seed of Eileen Chang’s Lust, Caution. The novel calls the gunmen Zhongtong agents, which accords with the fuller Chinese record — Zheng was run by Chen Baohua, the Zhongtong’s chief in Shanghai — though some English accounts loosely credit the rival Juntong. See the next note.

Two rival Nationalist secret services, named here by their chiefs. “Chen” means the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, whose CC Clique ran the Zhongtong (the party’s Bureau of Investigation and Statistics); “Dai” means Dai Li, who ran the Juntong (the military bureau). Ding is probing which service Lin serves; Lin’s reply refuses to say.

The Juntong — the Nationalists’ military Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, Dai Li’s secret service, seated in the wartime capital Chongqing. (The name dates strictly from 1938; the novel applies it across the whole period.) It kept standing lists of collaborators marked for death. Lin Nansheng and Gu Shenyan are its Shanghai agents.

The Wang Jingwei regime’s armed forces, in full the Peace National Construction Army (和平建国军), after Wang’s slogan of “peace and national reconstruction.” To Chongqing it was a collaborationist force. Historical.

Miss Lan is a 交际花 — a celebrated society beauty of the demimonde, moving among wealthy and powerful men, a figure of glamour and scandal. Her likeness on “calendar posters” (月历牌) refers to the hugely popular Shanghai advertising calendars of the era, on which fashionable women were painted to sell everything from cigarettes to patent medicine.
The Cathay Hotel (华懋饭店) on the Bund, part of Victor Sassoon’s Sassoon House and the most fashionable hotel in the city; today the north building of the Peace Hotel. Historical.

Xiaguan, the riverside district of Nanjing, saw ferocious fighting and mass killing when the city fell to the Japanese in December 1937 — the Nanjing Massacre. Miss Lan’s husband is among the Chinese soldiers who died there.

Chongqing, deep in the interior on the Yangtze, was the Nationalist government’s wartime capital after the loss of the eastern cities, and the seat of Dai Li’s Juntong. It was bombed relentlessly by Japanese aircraft throughout the war.
The idiom is 投石问路, literally to toss a stone to ask the road: a tentative probe thrown out ahead to see how the ground lies before one commits. The Reuters interview was the Juntong's stone.

ch01.anchor: Gu Shenyan poured him a glass of brandy
ch01.note: Gu Shenyan's given name, 慎言 (shèn yán), means “guarded in speech, watch your words” — a fitting name for a spymaster, and one the story quietly turns on. Chinese personal names carry plain lexical sense, and several in this book are chosen to tell.
The Red House (红房子) was a celebrated French restaurant in the Shanghai concessions and a fashionable place to be seen — cover enough, in itself, for two strangers to share a table before a killing.

ch02.note: The University of Shanghai (沪江大学), a Baptist missionary institution — hence the “disgrace before God” with which Zhu Yizhen’s mother threatens the principal. Historical.

Duoyunxuan (朵云轩), the celebrated Shanghai studio for painting, calligraphy, and seal-carving, founded in 1900; a seal-engraver trained there was a craftsman of standing. Ji Zhongyuan’s cover trade, a 装裱店, is a shop that mounts paintings and calligraphy onto hanging scrolls.
The Young Companion (良友), the best-known illustrated pictorial of Republican Shanghai (1926–1945), famous for its cover portraits of fashionable women. Historical.

The New Fourth Army Incident (皖南事变, the “Southern Anhui Incident”) of January 1941: Nationalist forces surrounded and destroyed the headquarters column of the Communist New Fourth Army, killing several thousand, though the two sides were nominally allied against Japan. It wrecked what remained of Nationalist–Communist cooperation, and is Zhu Yizhen’s reason to distrust a Juntong man. Historical.
The Type 97 (九七式) fragmentation grenade, standard issue in the Japanese army from 1937. Historical.

The idiom is 鱼龙混杂, “fish and dragons jumbled together”: a place where the worthy and the worthless, the honest broker and the cutthroat, mingle past telling one from another — the wartime concession exactly.

ch02.anchor: you within me, and me within you
ch02.note: A set phrase, 你中有我，我中有你, “in you there is me, in me there is you”: two services so riddled with each other's agents that they interpenetrate. Gu states the first law of the trade, and the novel proceeds to prove it on every side.

Zhu Yizhen's given name is 怡贞; Lin calls her by the doubled endearment 贞贞 (Zhenzhen). The 贞 means fidelity, constancy, a woman's chastity — a quiet irony to hang on a character who lives by divided loyalties, and between two men.

ch02.anchor: Ji Zhongyuan sat under the lamp
ch02.note: Ji Zhongyuan's given name, 中原 (Zhōngyuán), is the Central Plain, the ancient heartland of China — a resonant thing for a Communist agent to be called, and, like “Old Ji,” almost certainly a nom de guerre rather than the name he was born with.

ch03.note: Rue Ratard (巨籁达路), a plane-tree-lined street in the Shanghai French Concession, named for a French consul; today’s Julu Road. The concession setting is why the trees are “French.” In these years it still bore its French name. Historical.
The Battle of Shanghai (淞沪会战) of August–November 1937, the first great battle of the war against Japan, which laid waste much of the city and its outskirts. Historical.

Hongkou, north of Suzhou Creek, was the district where Shanghai’s large Japanese population was concentrated — the “Japanese quarter” of these chapters. Hongkou Park (today Lu Xun Park) lay at its heart. Historical.

Butterflies in Love with Flowers (蝶恋花), a set embroidery motif of butterflies among blossoms; the name, also that of a classical song-lyric tune, carries the sense of lovers drawn to each other. Zhu Yizhen’s return, again and again, to this one pattern is not incidental.

ch03.anchor: shrouded in horsehide on the field
ch03.note: “Shrouded in horsehide” renders 马革裹尸, from the Eastern Han general Ma Yuan, who vowed to die on the frontier and be carried home wrapped in a horse's hide rather than end in bed: the classic image of an honorable death in the field. Old Pan answers a real question with a slogan.

ch03.anchor: the dark spot under the lamp
ch03.note: The image is 灯下黑, “darkness beneath the lamp”: the ground directly under a lamp is the one place its light will not reach, so the safest hiding place is the one nearest the danger. Lin means the Japanese quarter, hidden under the occupier's own nose.
Tieguanyin (铁观音, “Iron Goddess of Mercy”), a prized oolong tea from Fujian.

ch04.note: The Blue Shirts Society (蓝衣社), a secret, fascist-influenced body of zealots within the Nationalist party, closely tied to Dai Li’s Juntong; here the collaborationist press uses the name to expose Chongqing’s Shanghai network. Historical.
The Zhonghua Ribao (中华日报), the chief newspaper of the Wang Jingwei regime. Historical.

HMS Peterel, a British river gunboat, was sunk in the Huangpu at Shanghai in the small hours of 8 December 1941 — hours after Pearl Harbor, across the international date line — when its captain refused a Japanese demand to surrender; six of the crew were killed. It was the sole act of armed resistance to the Japanese seizure of the International Settlement. Historical (the source’s transliteration of the name is preserved).
The Central Reserve Bank (中央储备银行), the note-issuing bank of the Wang Jingwei regime. Historical.

ch05.note: A garden mansion on Yuyuan Road, in the fashionable western district; such villas housed the senior men of the collaborationist regime and its secret service. Here it is Ding Mocun’s residence.

In the early 1930s Chiang Kai-shek directed his “encirclement and suppression” campaigns against the Communists from a field headquarters at Nanchang. That Gu Shenyan and Ding Mocun once served there together marks them as old comrades of the anti-Communist secret war — before Ding’s defection. Historical.

ch05.anchor: A man who is never dissolute wastes his youth
ch05.note: A saying, 人不风流枉少年: to pass one's youth without ever being dashing or dissolute is to waste it. Gu, the aesthete, offers it only half in jest.

ch06.note: The Indochinese Communist Party, founded in 1930 (Ho Chi Minh among its founders), was active among the Chinese and Vietnamese of Hong Kong and Indochina; Meng Annan’s planted cover has ripened into this deeper allegiance. Historical.

The Rectification Movement (整风运动), begun by the Communists at Yan’an in 1942 to enforce ideological conformity and weed out suspect cadres; its suspicion of outsiders is the opening Gu Shenyan means to exploit. Historical.

ch06.anchor: a stray stone, a dormant piece
ch06.note: A figure from the board game go (围棋): 闲棋冷子, a stone played early and left dormant, far from the fighting, to be activated much later when it decides the game. Gu Shenyan, a go player, means Meng Annan to lie unused in the enemy’s ranks for years.
Ta Kung Pao (大公报), a major and respected Chinese newspaper of the period. Historical.

The word rendered “rebel” is 叛逆者 (pànnìzhě), the novel's title. It is not the same as 叛徒 (pàntú), “traitor,” the word used of the turncoat Ding Mocun: a 叛逆者 is one who rebels, turns, breaks faith — a wider and more searching term, and the book's true subject, for it is Lin Nansheng's own allegiance that the war will unmake and remake.

“Dyed red” (染红): red is the color of the Communists, and to be dyed red is to have been won over to their cause and steeped in it. Ten years in the movement, Gu means, have made Meng one of them in fact, not merely in cover.
A kabushiki-gaisha (株式会社) is a Japanese joint-stock company. Under the occupation such a firm was a natural front for an intelligence post.

ch07.note: Hong Kong surrendered to Japan on 25 December 1941 — “Black Christmas” — after eighteen days of fighting; the “armistice” is the British capitulation. This scene falls on its first anniversary, Christmas 1942. Historical.
The Tokkō (特高, from 特別高等警察, the “Special Higher Police”) was the Japanese political and thought police, charged with counter-espionage and the suppression of dissent. Historical.

The Sino-American Cooperative Organization (SACO, 中美合作所), a joint Nationalist–United States intelligence and guerrilla-training body set up in 1943 under Dai Li and the U.S. naval officer Milton Miles, with headquarters outside Chongqing. Lin Nansheng is recalled to instruct there. Historical.

A 七律 (qīlǜ), a regulated verse of eight lines of seven characters each, in strict tonal and parallel form — the most exacting of the classical Chinese poetic forms. Its ostensibly innocent “Ode to the Plum Blossom,” run in a newspaper over a pen name, is a prearranged signal for contact.

The plum (梅) flowers in the last of the winter cold, before any other tree, and so stands in Chinese tradition for purity, endurance, and integrity kept under hardship. An “Ode to the Plum Blossom” run in a newspaper is at once an innocent cover and a loyalist's creed — the right poem to carry a call that must not look like one.

ch08.note: Mount Gele (歌乐山), in the hills west of Chongqing, was where the Nationalists and the joint Sino-American organization kept training grounds, offices, and a notorious secret prison. Historical.

ch08.anchor: peaches and plums fill the world
ch08.note: The idiom is 桃李满天下, literally “peaches and plums fill all under heaven”: a teacher's pupils (his “peaches and plums”) are everywhere, a tribute to how widely he has taught. Here it flatters Gu Shenyan, whose students reach even into the highest ranks.

ch08.anchor: the Eighth Route Army office at No. 50 Zengjiayan
ch08.note: Zengjiayan No. 50 (曾家岩50号) was the Communists' liaison office in wartime Chongqing, associated with Zhou Enlai and the Party's Southern Bureau; it operated openly during the united front against Japan and was kept under close Nationalist surveillance. Historical.

ch08.anchor: Song-dynasty printing of the Wangyou Qingle Ji
ch08.note: The Wangyou Qingle Ji (忘忧清乐集, “Collection of Pure Joy in Forgetting Cares”) is a Song-dynasty classic of go, among the oldest surviving printed go treatises, gathering opening patterns and endgame problems. Corroborated (its Song origin, c. 1100, is attested in Chinese and Western scholarship). Here it serves as the key text of a cipher. On go itself, see the earlier note.

The Japanese terror-bombing of Chongqing ran from 1938 to 1943 and ended with a final raid on 23 August 1943; the date is corroborated. The specific figure of fifty-four aircraft flying from Wuhan is the novel's, and could not be independently confirmed against the scholarship on the campaign.

ch08.anchor: gone to Yan'an, or to Nanjing
ch08.note: The two enemy destinations: Yan'an (延安), the Communists' wartime capital in northern Shaanxi, and Nanjing, the seat of Wang Jingwei's Japanese-sponsored government. For a Juntong man to defect to either would ruin both Gu and the officer set to watch him.

ch08.anchor: the Chinese Youth Communist Party in Europe
ch08.note: The Chinese Youth Communist Party (旅欧中国少年共产党), founded in Paris in 1922 by work-study students including Zhou Enlai and Zhao Shiyan, was the European branch that helped seed the Chinese Communist Party. Historical.

The Whampoa Military Academy (黄埔军校), founded near Guangzhou in 1924 with Chiang Kai-shek as commandant, trained the officer corps of both the Nationalist and (in its early united-front years) the Communist armies. Historical.

ch08.anchor: both Eastern Expeditions and in the Northern Expedition
ch08.note: The Eastern Expeditions (1925) crushed the warlord Chen Jiongming in Guangdong; the Northern Expedition (1926–1928) was the Nationalist campaign that defeated the northern warlords and nominally reunified China. Historical.

The purge (清党) of 1927, begun with Chiang Kai-shek's violent April 12 coup in Shanghai, expelled and massacred Communists within the Nationalist camp and ended the first united front. To “break with the Chinese Communists” then was to change sides in a bloodletting. Historical.

ch08.anchor: followed Dai Li into the Lixingshe
ch08.note: The Lixingshe (力行社, the “Vigorous Practice Society”), founded 1932, was the secret, fascist-influenced inner core of Chiang Kai-shek's loyalist organization and the seedbed of Dai Li's secret service; it stood at the center of the wider Blue Shirts (see the earlier note). Historical.

ch08.anchor: now called himself Ho Chi Minh
ch08.note: Ho Chi Minh (1890–1969), the Vietnamese revolutionary and future president of North Vietnam, used many names across his career, among them Nguyen Ai Quoc and Ho Quang; he adopted the name Ho Chi Minh around the time of his release. He was in fact imprisoned by Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists in Guangxi from August 1942 to September 1943, moved through many jails — so Gu's clandestine prison visit is grounded in real history. Corroborated. On the Indochinese Communist Party, see the earlier note.

ch08.anchor: our Expeditionary Force in the Burma-India theater
ch08.note: The Chinese Expeditionary Force fought the Japanese in Burma alongside British and American troops (1942, and again 1943–1945) to keep open China's overland supply lines. Historical.

ch08.anchor: a plum-blossom brand, with no second hand
ch08.note: The watch's brand is 梅花, “plum blossom” — the same flower as the cipher poem “Ode to the Plum Blossom” noted earlier, and Gu's recurring emblem. Its missing second hand quietly marks a man whose own time is running out.

ch09.note: Nylon stockings (玻璃丝袜, literally “glass-silk stockings”) were a coveted American luxury in wartime China, along with the chocolate — the small tribute the foreign officers paid the women they took.

ch09.anchor: roving orioles of the low song halls
ch09.note: The phrase is 流莺, “roving oriole,” an old literary euphemism for a streetwalker: a woman who solicits on the move, as the bird flits from branch to branch.

The idiom is 车水马龙, “carriages like flowing water, horses like a dragon”: a scene of dense, ceaseless traffic. The natural English keeps the bustle; the image is the coiling dragon of an unbroken line of horses.
The Central Bank of China (中央银行) was the Nationalist government's own central bank, not to be confused with the Wang Jingwei regime's Central Reserve Bank noted earlier. Historical.
A 牌楼 (or 牌坊): a free-standing ceremonial gateway of stone or wood, raised to mark a temple, a street, or an act of virtue. A fixture of the old Chinese townscape.

ch10.anchor: the campaign to punish the traitors
ch10.note: A 汉奸 (hànjiān) is a “traitor to the Han,” a Chinese who collaborated with the Japanese occupier; after the 1945 victory the Nationalist government tried and executed collaborators in a wave of treason cases. The word is distinct from the 叛逆者 of the novel's title, discussed in an earlier note. Historical.
The Jing'an Temple (静安寺), an ancient Buddhist temple in central Shanghai; the surrounding district and its main road take their name from it. Historical.

The Loyal and Patriotic Army (忠义救国军), formed by Dai Li in 1937 and later trained under the Sino-American Cooperative Organization, was the Juntong's guerrilla and paramilitary arm; its units were among the first Nationalist troops to enter Shanghai after the Japanese surrender. Corroborated.
The Chongqing negotiations of 1945 between the Nationalists and the Communists, which produced the “Double Tenth Agreement” but failed to avert the civil war. Historical.

ch10.anchor: two grasshoppers tied to one string
ch10.note: The idiom is 一条绳上的蚂蚱, “grasshoppers strung on one line”: two parties so bound together that neither can escape the other's fate. The image is of insects tied to a single thread — one jumps, both go.
Wartime Shanghai and the towns around it sheltered tens of thousands of European Jewish refugees; the German clinic and its Jewish proprietress-nurse reflect that real presence. Historical.

ch10.anchor: the back gate of Zhaofeng Park
ch10.note: Zhaofeng Park (兆丰公园) was known to foreigners as Jessfield Park — the same Jessfield that named the road where No. 76 stood; it is today's Zhongshan Park in western Shanghai. Corroborated.
Fabi (法币), the Nationalist government's legal-tender paper money, introduced in 1935; by the late 1940s runaway inflation had all but destroyed its value. Historical.
“The old home” (老家) is the underground's code for the Communist base area and Party center — the place an exposed agent is recalled to. It recurs through these chapters as a quiet euphemism.

ch10.anchor: We are here to rescue you
ch10.note: This is the language of the “Rescue Campaign” (抢救运动) of 1943, the coercive spy-hunting phase of the Yan'an Rectification (noted earlier), in which cadres were pressed by interrogation into false confessions of espionage; “rescue” was the campaign's own euphemism for the purge. Zhu is being told her imprisonment is for her own good. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: before you speak, you greet the person first
ch11.note: A child in China is taught to address an elder by the proper kin-title before speaking to them; Miss Lan is coaching her son in the courtesy. His flat “My papa died long ago” is a pointed refusal of it.

ch11.anchor: a wild chicken, an oil-bottle drag, a broom-star
ch11.note: The four insults for a woman like her: 破鞋, a “worn shoe” (a loose or adulterous woman); 野鸡, a “wild chicken” (an unlicensed prostitute); 拖油瓶, an “oil-bottle drag” (a child a woman brings with her into a remarriage, and so the burdened woman herself); 扫帚星, a “broom-star,” that is a comet, a bringer of ruin, a woman blamed for the deaths around her. The English keeps the images; each is a small verdict of the society on her.

ch11.anchor: Mr. Du to be our witness
ch11.note: Du Yuesheng (杜月笙, 1888–1951), boss of the Green Gang and the most powerful private man in Republican Shanghai, patron and power-broker across business, politics, and the underworld. To secure him as a wedding witness is a mark of how far Lin has risen. Historical.
In 1946 the wartime Juntong was reorganized as the Ministry of National Defense's Bureau of Secrecy, the 保密局 (Baomiju), the postwar Nationalist secret service. Historical.

ch11.anchor: sweep your grave, and every day
ch11.note: The rites of the dead: 扫墓, sweeping and tending the grave, especially at the Qingming festival, and 上香, the daily offering of incense. To be left to perform them is, in her vow, the one thing worth living for.

ch11.anchor: the Metropol Theater on Avenue Foch
ch11.note: Avenue Foch (福熙路) was a French Concession boulevard, today's Yan'an Middle Road. The clash the novel stages — between Nationalist military police (宪兵) and the civil police — reflects a real and chronic friction between the two forces in the postwar city, though this particular incident is the novel's own.

The film's title, 龙凤花烛, names the paired dragon-and-phoenix candles burned at a wedding — an emblem of marriage and good fortune, set with deliberate cruelty against the child's death in the same scene.
A 盆景 (penjing): the Chinese art of the miniature tree or landscape grown in a shallow tray, the older cousin of the Japanese bonsai.

ch11.anchor: guard the stump to wait for the hare
ch11.note: The idiom is 守株待兔, from a fable in the Han Feizi: a farmer once saw a hare run headlong into a tree stump and die, and ever after waited by the stump for another — to trust foolishly to luck, or, as here, to lie in wait for the quarry to deliver itself.

ch11.anchor: strike the mountain to startle the tiger
ch11.note: The idiom is 敲山震虎, “strike the mountain to shake the tiger”: to make a show of force at one remove, so as to intimidate an adversary or flush him into the open.

ch11.anchor: the Jiangsu Special Committee's, and the Comintern's
ch11.note: Meng lists the tangle of Communist intelligence lines then running in Shanghai: the Party's East China Bureau (华东局) and Jiangsu Special Committee, the center at Yan'an, and the Comintern — the Moscow-run Communist International. To verify a man across these separate lines risked crossing them and exposing both. Historical.

ch12.note: The word here is 叛徒, a turncoat who betrays his own side and comrades — distinct from the 汉奸 (collaborator with the foreign enemy) noted earlier, and from the 叛逆者 of the title. Old Pan chooses to wear the name of the first so that his mission may live.

ch12.anchor: a shuttle in the Communist intelligence network
ch12.note: The word is 梭子, a weaver's shuttle: a courier who plies back and forth across the network carrying its messages, as the shuttle runs the thread across the loom.

Gu Shunzhang (顾顺章) was the head of the Chinese Communist Party's own security and intelligence service; captured in 1931, he defected to the Nationalists, and his confessions exposed the underground and led to mass arrests, nearly destroying the Party's urban networks. He is the archetype the station chief invokes: the senior agent who sells out his own. Corroborated.

ch12.anchor: beat the grass and startle the snake
ch12.note: The idiom is 打草惊蛇, “beat the grass and startle the snake”: to act rashly and alert the very quarry you meant to take unawares.
The Paramount (百乐门), the great Art Deco dance hall on Bubbling Well Road, was an emblem of Shanghai's glittering nightlife from the 1930s. Historical.

ch13.note: The Dangui (丹桂), one of old Shanghai's celebrated opera houses, its lineage going back to the great teahouse-theaters of the late nineteenth century. Historical.

The Nineteenth Route Army (十九路军) put up the fierce, celebrated defense of Shanghai against the Japanese in the January 28 Incident of 1932. That Rong and Old Pan “resisted the Japanese together in Shanghai” places them in that fight. Historical.

A 义庄: a charitable hall, often maintained by a native-place association or lineage, that housed coffins and corpses awaiting burial or transport back to the dead person's home district — a standard provision for those who died away from home. Historical.

The intelligence Lin carries belongs to the Liaoshen Campaign (September–November 1948), the decisive Manchurian campaign of the civil war. The siege of Changchun (May–October 1948) blockaded and starved the Nationalist garrison into surrender; a deployment-and-reinforcement plan for the Liao–Shen theater was battle-turning material. Corroborated.

ch13.anchor: the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University
ch13.note: Kangda (抗大), the Communists' cadre-training academy at Yan'an, which schooled a generation of Party military and political officers. Historical.

Xibaipo (西柏坡), the village in Hebei that served as the Communist Party's central headquarters in 1948, from which Mao Zedong and the leadership directed the closing campaigns of the civil war. Historical.

ch13.anchor: a hawk Gu Shenyan set loose
ch13.note: The word is 鹞子, a sparrowhawk or falcon; in the trade it is an agent “let loose” to fly free under deep cover for years — the very thing Meng Annan turns out to be.
An 义子: a formally adopted, non-blood son. Gu Shenyan raised Meng Annan after the boy's parents died; Lin was Gu's student, Meng his foster son — “only, each of us chose his own road.”

Meng Annan's true Vietnamese name (阮志中). His parents were followers of Ho Chi Minh who had studied in France, where they met Gu Shenyan, and who died in a French colonial prison in Saigon when the boy was ten. Historical in kind: Vietnamese revolutionaries were widely jailed and killed under French rule in this period.

ch14.note: A Catholic mission school (圣类思中学): 类思 renders the Christian name Aloysius. Such foreign-run mission schools were common in and around Republican Shanghai.

The alias joins Lin's own surname to 秋明 — the given name of Zuo Qiuming (左秋明), the friend and fellow trainee who took his own life under interrogation rather than talk (Batch 1). Lin lives on under the dead man's name. A telling name the Chinese reader catches at once.

ch14.anchor: a village head in the town
ch14.note: A 保长 (baozhang), the headman of a bao — a unit of the old baojia system of mutual-surveillance household groupings, inherited from the Nationalist order and, for a time, kept on after 1949. Here the local baozhang is the informer. Historical.

ch14.anchor: her hair in a child's bob
ch14.note: A 童花头, the girlish “child-flower” bob with a straight fringe — the schoolgirl hairstyle that fixes Zhu Yizhen, in Lin's memory, as the student she was when they met.

ch14.anchor: to Resist America and Aid Korea
ch14.note: The Korean War mobilization: China entered the war in October 1950, and the “Resist America, Aid Korea, Defend Home and Country” (抗美援朝，保家卫国) campaign — with its patriotic donation drives for the Volunteer Army — swept the cities through 1950–1951. Historical.

ch14.anchor: the war of resistance against the French
ch14.note: The First Indochina War (1946–1954), in which Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh fought to end French colonial rule in Vietnam. Meng Annan asks to go home and join it. Historical.

ch14.anchor: the Third Field Army to the Fujian front
ch14.note: The People's Liberation Army's Third Field Army carried the civil war into the southeast in 1949, including the Fujian coast facing Taiwan. Historical.

ch15.note: In Shakespeare's Hamlet, Fortinbras is the prince of Norway, not Sweden; the source's “Swedish prince” (瑞典王子) is an error, rendered here as printed. Contradicted by the play. It is a minor role, which is why the boy cast in it has leisure to read the whole tragedy.

ch15.anchor: the front door of St. Thérèse's Church
ch15.note: St. Thérèse's Church (小德肋撒堂), a real Gothic-style Catholic church with twin bell towers, dedicated to St. Thérèse of Lisieux (the “Little Flower”); 德肋撒 is the traditional Catholic transliteration of Thérèse/Teresa. Built on Datong Road (today Datian Road) in what is now the Jing'an district, its foundation laid on St. Thérèse's day, 3 October 1930, and opened a year later. Historical.

The International Funeral Parlor (万国殡仪馆), opened 1926 at the corner of Jiaozhou and Xinzha Roads, was the best-known funeral home of Republican Shanghai; the funerals of the film star Ruan Lingyu and the writer Lu Xun were held there. Historical.

“Wild pheasant” renders 野鸡 (literally “wild chicken”), old Shanghai slang for an unlicensed streetwalker who solicited on the streets rather than working from a registered house. The wife is accusing her husband of visiting prostitutes on his rounds, not of piety.
The Chinese dead were traditionally laid out on a door lifted from its hinges (门板), used as a plain bier before the body was coffined.

The “soft local speech” is the Wu topolect of the Shanghai region (吴侬软语, literally “the soft, tender speech of Wu”), famed for its gentleness; the priest, who first served in the north, reads instead in a Tianjin accent, a comic incongruity a local reader hears at once.
A funeral custom: a coin (口含钱, the “mouth-held cash”) was placed in the mouth of the dead, variously explained as fare for the journey below or to keep the mouth from gaping.

The undertaker's 门腔 is an obscure funerary term, evidently a made replacement for the missing tongue so the corpse may “speak”; the phrase is uncommon and the rendering “mouth-piece” is provisional. His point follows plainly: with the tongue gone, the dead man cannot cry out his wrong (喊冤) in the courts of the underworld.

“Opening a skylight” (开天窗), here said to be gang slang for a killing that leaves a hole in the back of the skull. The phrase is attested in other senses (burglary through a roof; the blank a censor left in a newspaper), but its use as an execution method is not corroborated in the reference sources; given as the neighbors' talk.

“Planting a lotus” (种荷花) is attested Shanghai underworld argot for disposing of a victim in the Huangpu River. Paired here with “opening a skylight” as the gangs' private punishments (家法, “house law”). Corroborated at the level of popular gang-history writing.

ch16.note: In the seven-week mourning sequence a rite is held every seventh day; the seventh of these, on the forty-ninth day (7×7), is the “last seventh” (断七, literally “breaking the seven”), after which formal mourning ends. Corroborated.

ch16.anchor: the slave of a conquered country
ch16.note: “Slave of a conquered country” renders 亡国奴, a bitter wartime epithet for a people living under foreign conquest, one of the era's most charged words. The postman's refusal to become one is offered as the reason he died.

An Eight Immortals table (八仙桌) is a square hardwood table seating eight, named for the Eight Immortals of Daoist legend; it stood at the center of a household's main room, for meals, guests, and, as here, a boy's calligraphy practice.

Hongkou (虹口), the district north of Suzhou Creek, was the heart of Shanghai's Japanese settlement (“Little Tokyo”) and of its military and intelligence organs; the “special-service station” (特务机关) was such an organ. Historical.

ch17.anchor: A letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold
ch17.note: The postmaster quotes a famous line of Du Fu (杜甫), from “Spring View” (春望), written in 757 amid the An Lushan rebellion: 烽火连三月，家书抵万金 — “The beacon-fires have burned three months on end; a letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold.” Corroborated.

Huang Tingjian (黄庭坚, 1045–1105) was a leading Song poet and one of the great masters of calligraphy; to have copied his running-hand models marks the letter-writer as a cultivated man, not the ordinary correspondent a postman sees. Historical.

The Siming Apartments (四明公寓, part of the Siming Village lane compound) were built in 1932 as staff housing for the Siming Bank, in the French Concession on Rue Ratard (巨籁达路, named for a French consul; renamed Julu Road in 1966). Historical.

Yu Hongjun (俞鸿钧, 1898–1960; known in English as O.K. Yui) was mayor of Shanghai at the time of the 1937 Japanese invasion (formally from late July to mid-November 1937). Historical. The source prints his name 俞鸿均; the attested figure is 俞鸿钧, and the name is corrected here.
The clock tower of the Maritime Customs House on the Bund, whose Westminster-chiming clock (“Big Ching”) was completed in 1927, was one of the waterfront's chief landmarks. Historical.

The London plane trees that line the old French Concession streets are called 法国梧桐 (“French parasol-trees”) in Chinese; their leaf-canopy is a signature of that quarter of Shanghai and recurs through the story.

The 88th Division (八十八师) was a German-trained elite infantry division of the National Revolutionary Army, one of the units Chiang Kai-shek rushed to the 1937 Battle of Shanghai, where it took catastrophic losses. Historical.
Chen Sunong (陈素农, 1900–1983), a Whampoa Academy graduate, is recorded as major-general chief of staff of the 88th Division. A real officer; corroborated.

ch17.anchor: See a snake and you'll strike it rich
ch17.note: A folk belief: the snake, a “little dragon,” is read as an omen of a coming windfall (见蛇必发, “see a snake and you're sure to prosper”) — hence the lottery ticket. Corroborated as a common belief, though not a universal one; some regions read a snake as ill luck.

ch18.note: The Special Naval Landing Forces (海军陆战队), Japan's marine infantry, were garrisoned at Hongkou; their action opened the Battle of Shanghai on 13 August 1937. Historical. (The battle itself is noted earlier, at The Rebel, installment 3.)

Jintan are small aromatic medicinal pellets taken as a breath-freshener and pick-me-up. The source's 人丹 is the Chinese domestic brand, launched to answer the Japanese original 仁丹 (also “Jintan”), the two the subject of a Sino-Japanese trademark war. Material culture; corroborated.
They are playing Chinese chess (象棋). The chariot (車), which moves and captures in straight lines to any distance, is the game's most powerful piece, answering to the rook.

ch19.note: “Fourth Avenue” is Sima Road (四马路, literally “fourth horse road”), today Fuzhou Road; in the Republican era it was Shanghai's street of brothels, teahouses, and publishing houses at once. Historical.

ch19.anchor: the political commissar of the Songjiang detachment
ch19.note: A political commissar (政委) is the Communist Party's political officer within a military unit, ranking beside its commander; the Songjiang detachment was a Party-led guerrilla force in the countryside southwest of Shanghai.

The Kempeitai (宪兵), the Imperial Japanese Army's military police, were notorious in occupied China for torture and summary execution; they are distinct from the Tokkō, the special higher (political) police noted earlier in The Rebel. Historical.

The Shanghai Municipal Police of the International Settlement recruited Sikhs from the Punjab from 1884; their turbans (often described as red), beards, and height made them a fixture of the streets, and they drew the mocking nickname 红头阿三 (“red-turban number three”). Historical.

From the late 1930s Shanghai took in tens of thousands of Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Europe, being one of the few ports that required no visa; many settled in Hongkou. The stranger now in Su Lina's old flat is a quiet marker of that displacement. Historical.

ch19.anchor: sauced duck from Lu Gao Jian
ch19.note: Lu Gao Jian (陆稿荐) is a celebrated cooked-meats house of Suzhou origin, a “time-honored brand,” best known for its sauced pork and sauced (braised) duck (酱鸭). Material culture; corroborated.

ch20.note: A catty (斤) is the Chinese pound, in the Republican era standardized at about 500 grams (600 grams historically); half a catty is thus roughly half a pound of tea.
“Cement” renders 水门汀, the Shanghainese phonetic borrowing of the English word “cement,” a relic of the treaty-port pidgin; by extension it means a concrete pavement. Corroborated.

Biluochun (碧螺春, “green snail spring”) is a famous green tea from the Dongting hills by Lake Tai near Suzhou, ranked among China's finest; the measure is the tael (两), about 37 grams. Material culture; corroborated.

ch20.anchor: broken at the Battle of Changsha
ch20.note: The Battles of Changsha (长沙会战) were fought between 1939 and 1944. Historically the 88th Division's near-annihilation, and the famous remnant of “eight hundred,” belong not to Changsha but to the 1937 defense of Shanghai — the “Eight Hundred Heroes” (八百壮士) of the 88th's regiment at the Sihang Warehouse. The novel appears to transpose that episode onto Changsha; it is rendered here as the source has it, with the discrepancy noted.

The “Queen of the Dance World” (舞林皇后) was the title given the reigning dance-hostess, often decided by a paying ballot; the wartime “benefit dances” (募捐义舞) turned such contests to raising relief funds for the resistance.

ch20.anchor: when Wang Jingwei became Foreign Minister in 1935
ch20.note: Corroborated: Wang Jingwei held the Foreign Minister's portfolio, concurrently with the premiership, until he was shot and resigned in November 1935. (Wang Jingwei is noted more fully at The Rebel, installment 1.)

A concubine (姨太太) was a formally kept secondary wife; the polygynous household of the wealthy persisted well into the Republic despite the new Civil Code. Su Lina's refusal is a refusal of that place.

ch21.note: Seymour Road (西摩路), a road in the western part of Shanghai's International Settlement, today Shaanxi North Road (陕西北路); it ran through a mixed residential and commercial district. Geographic; historical.

The pistol is a 马牌撸子 (here written 橹子), literally a “horse-brand pistol” — Chinese slang of the period for a Colt automatic. 马牌 (“horse brand”) names Colt after the rampant colt of its trademark; 撸子 is a northern colloquial word for a handgun. A Colt was a prized, high-end weapon, hence Zhongliang's remark. The reference is rendered plainly in the text. Corroborated.

ch21.anchor: singsong girl who knows nothing of a fallen nation's grief
ch21.note: An allusion to Du Mu (803–852), “Mooring on the Qinhuai” (泊秦淮): 商女不知亡国恨，隔江犹唱后庭花 — “The singsong girl knows not the grief of a fallen kingdom; across the river she still sings ‘Flowers of the Rear Courtyard.’” The “Rear Courtyard Flower” was the decadent air associated with the last, doomed ruler of the Chen dynasty, and Du Mu's couplet became the classic reproach of those who revel while their country falls. Here it fixes Su Lina's cover: the frivolous kept woman, singing while the nation burns. Literary allusion; the poet is historical.

Kagoshima Bay, at the southern tip of Kyushu, was chosen by the Imperial Japanese Navy in the autumn of 1941 to rehearse the attack on Pearl Harbor: its setting — a city on a small plain, ringed by mountains, on a shallow bay — closely resembled Honolulu and Pearl Harbor, and there the airmen perfected the shallow-water aerial torpedo the attack required. Father Brown, matching the terrain of Kagoshima to a map of Honolulu, has grasped what is coming. The scene falls before the raid of 8 December 1941 (7 December in Hawaii), with which the next installment opens. Historically corroborated.

ch22.note: Longhua (龙华; also romanized Lunghwa), in Shanghai's southern outskirts. After Pearl Harbor the Japanese interned Allied civilians at the Longhua Civil Assembly Centre, set up on the campus of a former middle school; it is the camp of J. G. Ballard's Empire of the Sun. Mass internment of enemy nationals began in earnest only in 1943, and the source telescopes it to December 1941, the day of the attack, when the first arrests of “hostile” foreigners did begin. Historical; the date is compressed. (Longhua was also, in the 1927–37 years, the site of the Nationalist garrison's execution ground — a different chapter of the same place.)

Bridge House (桥楼), beside the Sichuan Road bridge over Suzhou Creek, was the Shanghai headquarters and prison of the Kempeitai, the Japanese military police; foreigners and Chinese suspected of anti-Japanese activity were held there in caged cells and tortured, and it became a byword for horror. The real building was about eight stories; the source's “thirteen-story” is rendered as printed. Historical.
The Japanese soldier's word, 八格 in the source, transcribes baka (馬鹿, “fool, idiot”) — the opening of the common curse bakayarō (八格牙路, “damned fool”). Corroborated.

Sir Mark Aitchison Young (1886–1974), Governor of Hong Kong, surrendered the colony to Japan on 25 December 1941 — “Black Christmas” — after eighteen days of fighting. The Japanese surrender was received by Lieutenant General Sakai Takashi (酒井隆, 1887–1946), who had commanded the assault; Sakai was later tried and executed as a war criminal in 1946. Historical. (The fall of Hong Kong was noted earlier in The Rebel; the two men are named here.)

ch23.note: The Shōwa emperor, Hirohito, was born on 29 April 1901; his birthday, Tenchōsetsu (天長節), was a national holiday marked with gun salutes and celebration. On that day in 1942 he turned forty-one. Historical.

ch23.anchor: the second year of the Xuantong reign
ch23.note: Xuantong (宣统) was the reign title of Puyi, the last Qing emperor; its second year was 1910. The postmaster is saying he entered the postal service in 1910 — the year before the dynasty fell. Historical.

Renders 三教九流, literally “the three religions [Confucianism, Buddhism, Taoism] and the nine schools [of the classical philosophers]” — a set phrase for people of every kind and station, high and low. The literal catalogue is lost in the natural English. Idiom.

ch23.anchor: served two terms as a provincial governor under the Daoguang emperor
ch23.note: The office is the 巡抚 (xunfu), the chief civil administrator of a Qing province, here rendered “provincial governor.” The Daoguang reign ran 1821–1850. That the Japanese should desecrate the graves of a family with such a pedigree is the wound behind the postmaster's tears. Historical.

ch24.anchor: the First District of the Special Municipality of Shanghai
ch24.note: In the summer of 1943 the Japanese formally handed the International Settlement — the foreign-run concession — to Wang Jingwei's Nanjing government, which folded it into the Chinese-administered city; the source names the district it became. The retrocession was a propaganda gesture: real authority stayed with the Japanese and their puppet regime. Historical.

ch24.anchor: the Blue Sky, White Sun, and Wholly Red Earth flag
ch24.note: The national flag of the Republic of China (青天白日满地红) — a white sun on a blue canton, against a red field. Wang Jingwei's collaborationist government flew the same flag (at first with a small yellow pennant reading “Peace, Anti-Communism, National Reconstruction,” later dropped); its appearance over occupied Shanghai marks the puppet regime's authority, not a Nationalist one. Historical.

储备券, the banknotes of the Central Reserve Bank of Wang Jingwei's regime (the bank was noted earlier in The Rebel) — the paper money of occupied Shanghai. Wartime inflation steadily ate away their worth. Historical.

三炮台 was the Chinese name for Three Castles, a Virginia-tobacco brand of W. D. & H. O. Wills widely sold in Republican Shanghai; the Chinese name, literally “three gun-platforms,” renders the three castles of the English trademark. A premium foreign cigarette — the small luxury Su Lina leaves with each visit. Brand corroborated.

清乡 (qingxiang, “purifying the countryside”) was the joint Japanese and Wang-regime campaign, at its height from 1941, to wrest the rural districts around Shanghai from Communist and other resistance forces through blockade lines, household registration, and sweeps. The “winter plan” here is aimed at the New Fourth Army's base areas in central Jiangsu. Historical.

The shikumen (石库门, “stone-framed gate”) is the characteristic Shanghai lane-house: a row dwelling entered through a stone-framed doorway with heavy black wooden doors, opening off a communal alley. Material culture.

ch25.anchor: the warm nest of a pair of wild mandarin ducks
ch25.note: 野鸳鸯, literally “wild mandarin ducks.” Mandarin ducks (鸳鸯), which are believed to pair for life, are the Chinese emblem of wedded love; “wild” ones are a couple living together unwed, or illicitly. The image casts the safe-house as the nest of two who only pass as man and wife. Idiom and symbol.

ch25.anchor: Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, Central Executive Committee of the Chinese Nationalist Party
ch25.note: The card unmasks Qin Zhaokuan as an agent of the Zhongtong (中统) — the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Nationalist Party's Central Executive Committee, the intelligence organ of the CC Clique run by the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, established in its final form in 1938 and the party rival to Dai Li's military Juntong. The suave collaborator was a deep-cover Nationalist all along; the enameled Blue Sky, White Sun badge is the Nationalist party emblem, his token of identity. Historical.

ch25.anchor: take the two bullets he had caught for a self-inflicted ruse
ch25.note: 苦肉计, the “self-torture stratagem,” one of the classic Thirty-Six Stratagems: to wound oneself in order to win an enemy's trust. Qin means the Japanese will read his two wounds as a sacrifice he staged to prove his loyalty and clear himself of complicity. Idiom and allusion.

ch25.anchor: the dying sun was red as blood
ch25.note: The image echoes the closing line of Mao Zedong's lyric “Loushan Pass” (忆秦娥·娄山关, February 1935): 苍山如海，残阳如血 — “The blue mountains like a sea, the setting sun like blood.” That the memory of a dying Nationalist agent should carry a Communist poet's most famous image is a quiet irony of the book. Literary allusion; corroborated.

ch26.note: Qingming (清明, “Pure Brightness”), the tomb-sweeping festival, falls about 4–5 April; families sweep the ancestral graves and burn spirit-money. In the country a temple fair (庙会) often follows, its high point a procession that carries the local deity — here a Buddhist bodhisattva — through the streets on a sedan chair amid gongs and pipes. Such fairs are a genuine folk-religion custom, though the sedan-borne procession belongs to temple festivals at large rather than to Qingming alone. Folk custom (corroborated).

Korea was a Japanese colony from 1910. In the last years of the war Japan drew Koreans into its forces on a growing scale — a volunteer scheme from 1938, then outright conscription of twenty-year-old men from December 1944 — and some two hundred thousand Koreans served, many as labor or low-grade infantry. That a garrison’s “Japanese” were really pressed Korean conscripts is thus entirely plausible. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Korea under Japanese rule”).

St. Mary’s Hall (圣玛利亚女校/女中), an elite Episcopal girls’ school in Shanghai, formally so named in 1881 and famous for its English and its wealthy pupils (the writer Eileen Chang graduated in 1937). The source prints the non-standard 圣玛丽公学院; the school’s established English name is St. Mary’s Hall. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “St. Mary’s Hall, Shanghai”).

Yuan Shikai (袁世凯, 1859–1916), the first President of the Republic of China, ruled autocratically, outlawed the Nationalist Party after the failed “Second Revolution” of 1913, and in 1915–16 tried to make himself emperor. His regime jailed and killed political opponents; that Su Lina’s revolutionary parents died in one of his prisons sets her orphaning in those years. Historical (corroborated: Encyclopædia Britannica, “Yuan Shikai”).

ch26.anchor: throwing down his pen for the army
ch26.note: The phrase renders 投笔从戎, “to throw down the writing-brush and follow the army,” a set idiom for a scholar who quits his studies to soldier. It alludes to the Later Han general Ban Chao (32–102 CE), who is said to have flung down his copyist’s brush, declaring that a man should win honor in far countries rather than grow old over documents. The allusive image is lost in plain English; the note keeps it. Literary allusion (corroborated).

ch26.anchor: the Xuefeng Mountain campaign at Zhijiang
ch26.note: The Battle of West Hunan, or Battle of the Xuefeng Mountains (雪峰山战役, 9 April–7 June 1945), turned back a Japanese drive on the airfield at Zhijiang (芷江) in western Hunan; a decisive Chinese victory, it was the last great battle of the war against Japan. Zhijiang was where the Japanese sued for surrender that August (芷江受降). Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Battle of West Hunan”).

ch26.anchor: a history student at Nanhua University
ch26.note: No university named Nanhua (南华大学) existed in wartime Republican China; institutions of that name are of much later date (a Taiwan university founded 1996; a Hunan university formed by merger in 2000). The company commander’s alma mater has no identifiable wartime referent and appears to be the author’s invention or an anachronism. Uncorroborated as a historical institution (checked: Wikipedia, “Nanhua University”; “National Southwestern Associated University”).

The headman (保长) was the lowest official of the baojia (保甲) system, an old scheme of household registration and collective responsibility revived by the Nationalists: households were grouped into jia and jia into bao, each under a headman answerable for taxes, labor levies, and reporting on his neighbors. Historical (Republican local control).

ch26.anchor: half a silver dollar for every household
ch26.note: The silver dollar (大洋, “big ocean,” i.e. the silver yuan / 银元) was the hard coin of Republican China, worth far more than the collapsing paper notes; half a dollar per household on a postman’s round was a modest but real fee. Historical (money).

ch27.anchor: routed from the Yangtze defense line
ch27.note: In April 1949 the People’s Liberation Army forced the Yangtze in the Crossing-the-River Campaign, breaking the Nationalists’ river line and taking Nanjing; Shanghai fell after a fortnight’s fighting in late May 1949. The rout pouring into the city here is that collapse. Historical (the 1949 Yangtze crossing and Shanghai campaigns).

Tilanqiao Prison (提篮桥监狱), built 1901–03 in the International Settlement and once among the largest prisons in the world (“the Alcatraz of the Orient”), known in English as Ward Road Gaol. After 1945 it held Japanese war criminals and Chinese collaborators of the Wang Jingwei regime; a U.S. military court sat inside it in 1946. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Tilanqiao Prison”).

ch27.anchor: a member of the anti-war league
ch27.note: The Japanese People’s Anti-war Alliance (日本人民反战同盟) was formed in December 1939 at Guilin, largely from captured Japanese soldiers who had turned against the war, under the writer Kaji Wataru; a parallel body, the Japanese People’s Emancipation League under Nosaka Sanzo, re-educated prisoners at Yan’an from 1944. Itō’s claim to have joined in 1944 is his passport under the new order. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Japanese People’s Anti-war Alliance”).

ch27.anchor: toll the bell for the day
ch27.note: A rendering of the proverb 做一天和尚撞一天钟, “a monk for a day tolls the bell for a day” — to do one’s work perfunctorily, drifting through each day with no thought for the next. The postmaster means the office may close at any time. Idiom (corroborated: 汉典).

The Waibaidu Bridge (外白渡桥), known in English as the Garden Bridge, spans Suzhou Creek at its mouth beside the Bund; the present steel truss, opened in 1908, was the first all-steel bridge in China. The name means the “outer toll-free ford.” Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Waibaidu Bridge”).

The China Merchants Steam Navigation Company (轮船招商局, founded 1872 by Li Hongzhang) was China’s first modern steamship line, an “officially supervised, merchant-managed” enterprise with wharves and godowns along the Huangpu. Its riverside warehouses were prizes in the street fighting for Shanghai. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “China Merchants Group”).

ch28.note: The Five-Starred Red Flag (五星红旗) was adopted on 27 September 1949 and first raised over Tiananmen on 1 October 1949, at the founding of the People’s Republic. Flying everywhere on “the first day of the new year,” it dates the scene to New Year 1950. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Flag of China”).

ch28.anchor: going up and down the streets in a green hat
ch28.note: The joke turns on 戴绿帽子, “to wear a green hat,” Chinese slang for a man whose wife is unfaithful — a cuckold. The postmen’s new green caps make them, in the ribald phrase, walking cuckolds. The idiom’s exact origin is disputed (green long marked low or brothel status), but its cuckold sense is old and universally understood; the pun cannot survive a literal English rendering. Idiom (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Green hat”).

Shilin cloth (士林布) is cotton dyed with Indanthren, a German synthetic vat-dye famed for not fading; indanthrene blue was everywhere in 1930s–40s China, in gowns and school uniforms alike — “the cloth that never fades.” On Su Lina, once queen of the dance, the plain faded stuff marks how far she has fallen. Historical (material culture; corroborated).

The exchange marks a real change of address. Nationalist and warlord armies called a superior 长官 (zhǎngguān, “officer”); the Communist forces used 首长 (shǒuzhǎng, “chief”), tied to their doctrine of equality between officers and men, 长官 carrying for them a taint of high-handedness. Su Lina, asking for a 长官, is corrected into the new vocabulary. Historical (corroborated).

ch28.anchor: on the way back to the Soviet area
ch28.note: The Soviet area (苏区) meant the base regions held by the Communists and their armies — here a rear district the underground was withdrawing to. Suqian (宿迁) is a town in northern Jiangsu. Historical (Communist base areas).

ch29.note: Pan Hannian (潘汉年, 1906–1977) was the Communists’ foremost intelligence officer in the Shanghai underground — the very world of these stories — and, after 1949, a Deputy Mayor of Shanghai. In 1955 he was suddenly arrested and accused of secret dealings with the Japanese and with the traitor Wang Jingwei; he was imprisoned and died in disgrace in 1977, and only in 1982 was the case declared a fabricated miscarriage of justice. That Zhongliang appeals to him to lift a false treason charge from his wife is bitterly ironic. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Pan Hannian”).

Chen Yi (陈毅, 1901–1972), one of the ten Marshals of the People’s Republic, was the first mayor of Shanghai after its capture in 1949 and later China’s foreign minister. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Chen Yi (marshal)”).

ch29.anchor: Luo Ruiqing, the Minister of Public Security
ch29.note: Luo Ruiqing (罗瑞卿, 1906–1978), a senior PLA general, was the first Minister of Public Security of the People’s Republic, appointed in October 1949. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Luo Ruiqing”).

ch29.anchor: the first National Day of New China
ch29.note: National Day (国庆节) falls on 1 October, the anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic on 1 October 1949; the “first National Day” is thus that of 1 October 1950, dating Zhou Chukang’s visit to the autumn of 1950. Historical.

Pasting matchboxes at home was classic piece-work handed out through the neighborhood (street) committees of the early People’s Republic, often to those without regular jobs or under a political cloud — as Su Lina, a marked “spy suspect,” is. The detail measures her reduced life. Social custom (early PRC).

ch29.anchor: airlifted from India to Shanghai to take the surrender
ch29.note: After Japan’s surrender in August 1945, United States aircraft ferried Nationalist troops — among them forces of the Chinese Expeditionary Force returning from the India–Burma theater — to the coastal cities to accept the Japanese surrender before the Communists could reach them. Historical (the 1945 airlift to reoccupy the east).

Siping (四平), a rail city in the Northeast, was fought over repeatedly in the civil war of 1946–48. To “lead his men over” renders 起义, the battlefield defection of a Nationalist unit to the Communist side, a standard event of those years. Zhou Chukang’s Fourth Field Army (第四野战军, Lin Biao’s army, grown from the Northeast forces) went on to sweep south. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Battle of Siping”).

ch29.anchor: the first deputy division commander of the Volunteer Army to fall on the Korean battlefield
ch29.note: The Chinese People’s Volunteer Army entered the Korean War in October 1950. The claim that Zhou Chukang was the first deputy division commander (副师长) to die there is the novel’s own; standard accounts single out division chiefs of staff, not deputy commanders — Hu Qianxiu (胡乾秀), chief of staff of the 58th Division, killed at Chosin on 20 December 1950, is usually named the earliest senior officer lost. Rendered faithfully; the specific “first” is uncorroborated (checked against Chinese accounts of PVA officers killed in Korea).

ch30.note: The detail is left unexplained, but its resonance would be plain to a Chinese reader: “twenty years later” places the scene around 1970, in the Cultural Revolution (1966–76), when those denounced at struggle-sessions were commonly shaved — often the humiliating half-shaved “yin-yang head.” Su Lina, forever tainted as a former spy and a collaborator’s mistress, is destroyed in that last persecution. The reading is strongly implied rather than stated. Historical resonance.

蝇头小楷, literally “fly’s-head small regular script,” is the term for minutely fine 小楷 (small standard-script) calligraphy. It recalls the bookish, copperplate-loving Zhongliang of the story’s opening, now writing his dead wife letters no one will read. Idiom / nuance (corroborated).

ch31.note: “Devils” (guizi) was the standard wartime Chinese epithet for the Japanese; “running dog” (zougou, here “lackey”) for one who served them. Unable to place a Korean prisoner, the interrogator reaches for both at once. Texture.

The Battle of Wuhan (June–October 1938) was the largest engagement of the war's early years; Japanese forces took the city on 27 October 1938, and the Nationalist government, already withdrawn upriver, made Chongqing its wartime capital in earnest. Wuhan is the union of three towns on the Yangtze — Wuchang, Hankou, and Hanyang. Historical (corroborated).

ch31.anchor: taking back the Japanese concession in Hankou
ch31.note: Hankou held a cluster of foreign concessions; the Japanese one dated from 1898. After full-scale war broke out in 1937 its Japanese residents withdrew, and on 13 August 1938 the Nationalist government took the concession over as the Hankou No. 4 Special Zone — the event the story places “a year after the Battle of Shanghai.” Japan reclaimed it on occupying the city that October and in 1943 nominally ceded it to the Wang Jingwei regime. Historical (corroborated).

Kyoto Imperial University (founded 1897) was one of imperial Japan's two oldest and most prestigious universities, its medical faculty among the finest in the empire. That a colonial Korean holds such a degree is the very thing the Japanese officer later trades on. Historical.

Kim Ku (1876–1949), leader of the Korean independence movement and a head of the Provisional Government in exile. On 7 May 1938, at a gathering of Korean parties in the Nammok Hall in Changsha, a disaffected Korean, Yi Un-han, opened fire; one delegate was killed and Kim Ku gravely wounded, though he survived. This is the “shooting in Changsha.” Historical (corroborated).

ch31.anchor: the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea
ch31.note: The Korean Provisional Government, formed in Shanghai in 1919 after the March First independence movement, was the exile government of the Korean cause; through the war it moved with the Chinese Nationalists across the country — Changsha, then Chongqing — which is why its adherents turn up here in wartime China. Historical (corroborated).

The priest's phrase renders the idiom luoye guigen, “fallen leaves return to their roots” — the wish to die and be buried in one's native soil. In his mouth it is doubled: a Korean exile's longing for a homeland under Japanese rule, and the reason he serves the independence cause behind his cassock. Idiom (texture).

The “Expeditionary Army” (pai-qian jun) is the Japan China Expeditionary Army, the command for Japanese forces in China. As a colonial subject of the empire, Jiang is liable to its call-up, and refusal, as the officer implies, carried grave penalties. Historical.

ch31.anchor: So her name was Tang Ya
ch31.note: Her given name, Ya (雅), means “refined, elegant, cultivated” — the word for a lettered young woman, apt for the Chinese-literature student she was. The novella will set that name against what the war makes of her, a bar-haunting executioner; the irony is there for a Chinese reader at the first sight of the character. Texture (telling name).

ch32.note: A documented detail: after taking Wuhan the Japanese army turned the National Wuhan University campus at Mount Luojia (the story's “Wuchang University”) into a hospital for its wounded, and in the spring of 1939 planted the first cherry trees there to ease the men's homesickness. Those trees are the origin of the university's now-famous cherry blossoms. Historical (corroborated).

“Shina” (Chinese Zhina) was the name Japan used for China in this period. Neutral in origin, it became in imperial and wartime usage a term of contempt, rejected by the Chinese as a slur. The propaganda headline's “in Shina” is the occupier's word for the country it is invading. Historical (corroborated).

The “Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere” was Japan's slogan for the bloc of Asian territories it claimed to be freeing from Western rule and uniting under its own leadership — in practice the ideological cover for conquest. A Korean doctor tending Chinese poor made ideal propaganda for it. Historical (corroborated).

The Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun (1872–1943) was one of Japan's major dailies, tied to the Osaka Mainichi and a forerunner of today's Mainichi Shimbun; in the war years it carried the army's line. Historical (corroborated).

ch32.anchor: a great man can bend and can stretch
ch32.note: The proverb da zhangfu neng qu neng shen, “a great man can bend and can stretch” — that is, endure humiliation now to prevail later, a maxim of strategic patience. The priest uses it to keep Jiang inside the enemy's uniform. Idiom (texture).

From the set phrase tiao jin Huang He ye xi bu qing, “even leaping into the Yellow River you couldn't wash yourself clean” — said of a disgrace or suspicion no protest can rinse away (the Yellow River runs thick with silt). Jiang means his complicity is now indelible. Idiom (texture).
The meiyu, or “plum rains” — the long, humid rainy season of the middle and lower Yangtze in early summer, named for its coincidence with the ripening of the plums. Climate / custom.

Potassium cyanide, a fast-acting poison, was the agent's standard means of suicide on capture; here it is sealed in wax inside a hollowed silver dollar, the piece of tradecraft the novella takes for its title. Guo will later call it “the last gift a killer keeps for himself.” Note that it is passed as a means of self-destruction, not of murder — the axis on which the plot turns. Historical / motif.

ch33.note: The Pacific War opened with Japan's attacks on Pearl Harbor and Southeast Asia in December 1941, bringing the United States into the conflict; wartime Chongqing filled with American servicemen and correspondents, the clientele the bar reflects. Historical (corroborated).

“The Hump” was the airlift route Allied transports flew over the eastern Himalayas from India to supply Nationalist China after the Burma Road was cut in 1942 — punishing, high-altitude flying with heavy losses. The young captain has just crossed it. Historical (corroborated).

The Central Police Academy (Nanjing, 1936) trained the Nationalists' police officers. Chiang Kai-shek was its titular head, but Dai Li — chief of the Juntong, the military secret service — ran it as superintendent and used it, as the passage says, to recruit young cadets into the Juntong and plant them through the government. So a graduate of the academy might well be a Juntong agent in disguise, which is why Guo distrusts Tang Ya. Historical (corroborated).

ch33.anchor: mend the fold after the sheep is lost
ch33.note: The chengyu wang yang bu lao, “to mend the fold after the sheep are lost” — to repair a fault after harm is done, before worse follows; usually reassuring, “better late than never.” Guo turns it cold, on the loose end Tang Ya represents. Idiom (texture).

ch33.anchor: What youth is not moved by love
ch33.note: Guo quotes, in colloquial form, a couplet Chinese readers know from Guo Moruo's celebrated translation of Goethe's The Sorrows of Young Werther: roughly, “What young man is not stirred to love? What maiden does not yearn in spring?” A worldly, faintly mocking gloss on the bond he suspects between Jiang and Tang Ya. Allusion (corroborated).

ch33.anchor: the twenty-seventh year of the Republic
ch33.note: Dates in Republican China were counted from the founding of the Republic in 1912, so “the twenty-seventh year of the Republic” is 1938, the year Wuhan fell. Historical (corroborated).

ch34.anchor: the air-raid tunnel disaster at Jiaochangkou
ch34.note: The Jiaochangkou tunnel disaster (5 June 1941): during a prolonged Japanese night raid on Chongqing, huge crowds packed into a public shelter near Jiaochangkou whose entrances were kept sealed, and mass suffocation and trampling followed — the deadliest single incident of the Chongqing bombing. The toll is disputed: Nationalist figures put it near a thousand, later accounts at 2,500 or more, and popular memory (like the source's “tens of thousands”) far higher. The exact number was never fixed. Historical (corroborated; toll contested).

The Hanyang Arsenal, founded in the 1890s by the reformer Zhang Zhidong, was China's oldest modern ordnance works and the maker of the “Hanyang-made” rifle carried through decades of war; like much of China's industry it was dismantled and shipped west, up the Yangtze, ahead of the Japanese advance. Historical (corroborated).

In the wartime capital the Nationalist government issued bans on dance halls and public amusements (the jin yu ling, “ban on entertainment”) as unbecoming a nation at war — which is how the raids that shut the halls brought Tang Ya to Yang Qun's notice. Historical.

ch34.anchor: watching the stump for a hare
ch34.note: The chengyu shou zhu dai tu, “to watch the tree stump waiting for a hare” — from the fable of a farmer who, having once seen a hare run into a stump and die, gave up his plow to wait by it for another. It means to sit idle for a windfall; Tang Ya turns it on the men lying in wait for Jiang. Idiom (texture).

ch34.anchor: a worn shoe on another man's foot
ch34.note: “A worn shoe” (po xie) is Chinese slang for a woman of loose reputation. Old Jin's silent pity is exactly this: he sees Tang Ya throwing herself away, and the phrase carries the judgment even as he grieves it. Slang (texture).

ch35.note: The story has the Zhongtong — the Nationalist Party's civil secret service — keep its known office, a mere signboard, at the East Sichuan Normal School, while its real work is done in an unmarked house by the wharf. Hiding the working headquarters behind a public front was standard tradecraft for both Nationalist services; the specific placement here is the novella's, not a matter of record. Institutional (plausible).
Chaotianmen, at the tip of the peninsula where the Jialing River meets the Yangtze, is Chongqing's oldest and largest wharf and the water gateway to the mountain city. Geographic (corroborated).

Tieguanyin (“Iron Goddess of Mercy”) is a prized oolong from Anxi county in Fujian; “spring water, autumn fragrance” evokes its seasonal picking. By pouring Yang Qun the tea of his own birthplace, Guo shows without a word how thoroughly he has read the man's file. Material culture (corroborated).

ch35.anchor: a fish that slipped the net
ch35.note: The chengyu lou wang zhi yu, “a fish that slipped through the net” — one who escapes a dragnet. Guo means Jiang's corpse, which Yang Qun is to “discover” with a scalpel planted on it, so the killing of the American passes as the work of a Japanese spy run to ground. Idiom (texture).

ch35.anchor: lick blood from the knife's edge
ch35.note: Dao tou tian xue, “to lick blood from the edge of the knife” — to live by killing, a hair from death; the trade of the assassin. Guo invokes the danger of their calling to justify letting Jiang keep the woman. Idiom (texture).

ch35.anchor: a needle at the bottom of the sea
ch35.note: From the proverb nuren xin, hai di zhen — “a woman's heart is a needle at the bottom of the sea,” impossible to fathom or to retrieve. Guo's parting word undercuts his own generosity: he has handed Jiang the woman, but not her heart. Proverb (texture).

“Lukewarm water” (wen-tun shui) is said of a tepid, spineless person who will neither boil nor freeze. It is Tang Ya's contemptuous name for Yang Qun's unshakable, fatherly patience — the very evenness she wants to crack. Idiom (texture).

ch36.note: The Japanese national flag, a red sun-disc on white (the Hinomaru). Chinese wartime slang called it the 膏药旗, the “plaster flag,” because the red disc looked like a round medicinal plaster stuck to a white cloth. Historical.

The Type 38 (三八式) infantry rifle, the standard Arisaka bolt-action rifle of the Japanese army, named for the 38th year of the Meiji era (1905), when it was adopted. It was unusually long, so that with the bayonet fixed it stood taller than the short soldiers who carried it, as the passage notes. Historical.

The Three People’s Principles Youth Corps (三民主义青年团), the Nationalist party’s youth organization, founded in 1938; its cadre training classes drilled young officials and officers. In southern Jiangxi it fell under the reforming administration of Chiang Kai-shek’s son (see the next chapter). Historical.

ch36.anchor: the raid on the Huangshan residence last year, on the thirtieth of August
ch36.note: Chiang Kai-shek kept several official residences in wartime Chongqing; the villa on Huangshan (Mount Huang), east of the city, served as his command retreat. Japanese aircraft raided it in August 1941 while he was chairing a conference of his generals, a near-miss “decapitation” strike. The source dates the raid to 30 August, rendered as printed. Corroborated (the August 1941 raid); the exact day is not independently confirmed here.

ch36.anchor: the Korean Liberation Army, under General Yi Cheong-cheon
ch36.note: The Korean Liberation Army (한국광복군; 光复军, literally the army of “recovered light”) was the military arm of the Korean Provisional Government, founded in Chongqing on 17 September 1940 with Nationalist Chinese backing. Its first commander-in-chief was Ji Cheong-cheon (지청천); the source’s 李青天 renders his adopted surname, and he is also known as Yi Cheong-cheon. Historical (corroborated).

ch36.anchor: two Mausers, one in either hand
ch36.note: The Mauser C96 (驳壳枪, the “box cannon”), a broom-handled semi-automatic pistol often carried in a wooden holster that doubled as a shoulder-stock. Cheap, plentiful, and iconic in the Chinese wars of the era. Historical.

ch37.note: The “Youth-Cadre class” (青干班, short for 青年干部训练班) was a training course for young Nationalist officials and officers, run here under Chiang Ching-kuo’s Gannan administration, the setting of this chapter. Historical.

The phrase is 世外桃源, a “Peach-Blossom Spring beyond the world”: from Tao Yuanming’s fifth-century fable of a fisherman who stumbles on a hidden valley at peace, untouched by the wars outside. It has meant an idyllic refuge ever since. Allusion (corroborated).

The bathhouse borrows the name of the Huaqing Pool (华清池), the imperial hot springs near Xi’an where the Tang emperor Xuanzong bathed with his consort Yang Guifei, a byword for languorous pleasure. The joke is that a smugglers’ bathhouse in reforming, dry Gannan should wear so voluptuous a name. Allusion (historical).

ch37.anchor: he no longer knew where he would sober up, or when
ch37.note: The line echoes a celebrated couplet by the Song lyricist Liu Yong (柳永): “Where shall I sober tonight? A bank of willows, the dawn wind, a waning moon.” It has become shorthand for the drinker’s drifting, solitary melancholy. Allusion (corroborated).

ch37.anchor: Chiang Ching-kuo brought his New Deal to Gannan
ch37.note: Chiang Ching-kuo (蒋经国, 1910–1988), Chiang Kai-shek’s elder son and a future president of Taiwan, administered the Gannan region of southern Jiangxi from 1939 to 1945. His reforming “New Deal” (新政) banned prostitution, opium, and gambling; within a year, the sources agree, the region’s brothels had closed. The conventional Wade–Giles spelling of his name is used. Historical (corroborated).

ch37.anchor: A wartime wife is a wife too
ch37.note: 抗战夫人, a “wartime wife”: the common arrangement by which a man cut off from his family by the fighting took a second, de facto wife where he was posted. The phrase names a whole social phenomenon of the refugee years, half tolerated and half winked at. Cultural (historical).
A proverb, 人走茶凉: “when the man leaves, his tea goes cold” — warmth and attention last only as long as one’s presence or use. Shen Jinzhu turns it on the dead. Idiom.
Doenjang-guk (大酱汤), a Korean stew built on fermented soybean paste, the everyday soup of a Korean household. Jiang, a Korean from Jeju, cooks it as the taste of home. Cultural.

ch37.anchor: Jeju Island, where he was born
ch37.note: Jeju (제주도; 济州岛), the large volcanic island off the southern coast of Korea, is Jiang Yongnan’s birthplace. Geographic.

ch38.note: The Youth Army (青年军) was a corps of educated volunteers raised by the Nationalists in 1944 under the recruiting slogan “a hundred thousand youths, a hundred thousand soldiers.” Its divisions were numbered from 201; the 207th, formed on 1 January 1945, was among the few to see hard fighting. Historical (corroborated).

“The Generalissimo” (委员长, literally the Chairman of the Military Affairs Commission) was the standard wartime title for Chiang Kai-shek, head of the Nationalist government and supreme commander of its armies. Historical.
The Military Affairs Commission (军委会, 军事委员会) was the Nationalist government’s supreme organ of military command throughout the war, chaired by Chiang Kai-shek. Historical.

ch38.anchor: An inch of our rivers and hills for an inch of blood
ch38.note: “An inch of rivers and hills for an inch of blood” (一寸山河一寸血) was half of the couplet coined for the 1944 Youth Army recruiting drive; the other half ran “a hundred thousand youths, a hundred thousand soldiers.” Guo reads it off the medal on Jiang’s chest. Historical (allusion).

The Battle of Mount Song (松山战役), June to September 1944, was the ferocious assault by which the Chinese Expeditionary Force retook the fortified peak of Songshan in western Yunnan and reopened the Burma Road. The dug-in Japanese garrison fought nearly to the last man; Chinese losses ran to some four thousand dead. Historical (corroborated).

Mangyou renders 芒友 (Mong-Yu), the road junction in northern Burma where, in late January 1945, the Chinese Army in India and the Expeditionary Force from Yunnan met and reopened the overland supply route—the Stilwell Road—into China. Historical (corroborated).

A running-key or “book” cipher keys its message to the running text of an agreed book—here an English Hamlet—so that without the same edition (the 母本, the “key text”) the numbers cannot be read back into words. Yang Qun has had to reconstruct both the book and the English-to-Chinese step. Technical.

The Taiping Society (太平会) is offered here as rumor: a shadowy fraternity of Christian merchants and officials said to reach into every ministry. No such organization is historically attested; it is the novel’s own invention, and unrelated to the nineteenth-century Taiping Rebellion. Fictional (presented as legend).

ch39.note: The phrase is 连坐, the old principle of collective liability by which a criminal’s kin or associates were punished along with him—a recurring instrument of Chinese statecraft from the Qin dynasty onward. Jiang’s captors hold his brother’s family, still inside China, hostage against his silence. Historical (the legal principle).

Old Jin’s phrase is 摆龙门阵 (bǎi lóngménzhèn), Sichuanese for idle storytelling or shooting the breeze, literally “laying out the Dragon-Gate array.” It marks him, like his oaths, as a Sichuan man. Idiom (dialect).

除夕, the eve of the lunar New Year and the last day of the year, is the great family reunion of the Chinese calendar, kept with fireworks and red lanterns. The lanterns and fireworks of these closing scenes set Jiang’s execution and Tang Ya’s revenge against the most domestic of festivals. Cultural.

ch40.anchor: a grand return-to-the-capital ceremony at the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum in Nanjing
ch40.note: With Japan defeated, the Nationalist government moved its capital back from wartime Chongqing to Nanjing; the return (还都) was proclaimed on 5 May 1946. The Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum (中山陵), the monumental tomb of the republic’s founder on Purple Mountain east of Nanjing, was the natural site for such state ritual. Historical (corroborated: the return was declared 5 May 1946).

Qixia Temple (栖霞寺), on Qixia Mountain northeast of Nanjing, is one of the great Buddhist monasteries of the south, founded in the fifth century and famed for the Thousand-Buddha carvings on its cliff; during the 1937 massacre it sheltered thousands of refugees. Guo keeps his fast here on the very day of the capital’s triumphant return. Historical.
A 沙弥 (Sanskrit śrāmaṇera) is a novice monk, a boy or young man who has taken the preliminary vows but not yet full ordination. Historical (Buddhist).

The Chinese for a shot glass is 子弹杯, literally a “bullet cup.” The closing scene turns the idiom over quietly, given the cyanide coin, the sniper’s bullet, and the drink that shares the poison’s name. Wordplay lost in translation.
