ch41.note: Yanzhi (胭脂) is the ordinary Chinese word for rouge, the red cosmetic a woman reddens her cheeks and lips with. As a girl's given name it is at once pretty and faintly disreputable, the mark of a painted, sensual beauty rather than a virtuous one; the novella's title turns on it. (Nuance lost in translation.)

ch41.anchor: long life together and a fine son soon
ch41.note: The guests' parting words render two stock wedding blessings: 白头偕老, “may you grow white-haired together,” and 早生贵子, “may you soon bear a noble son.” Formulaic good wishes, spoken here over a marriage no one quite believes in. (Nuance.)

The cheongsam (旗袍, qipao) is the close-fitting, high-collared Chinese woman's dress, cut in one piece and slit at the side. Baosheng's whole trade is the making of them, and the dress, with the labor of sewing it, runs through the entire novella. Historical (dress).

The pankou (盘扣), the knotted cloth frog-buttons that fasten a cheongsam, are hand-coiled from a thin roll of fabric into ornamental shapes: butterflies, plum-blossoms, gourds. To work them in dozens of distinct patterns was the mark of a master tailor; the “seventy-two” is the family's boast, not a fixed catalogue. Cultural (material culture).

ch41.anchor: a hundred li around Jiahe County
ch41.note: A li (里) is the Chinese mile, about half a kilometre. “A hundred li around” is the common idiom for the whole surrounding region rather than an exact span. (Measure.)

Pingtan (评弹) is the storytelling-and-ballad art of Suzhou and the Jiangnan water towns: a performer, or a pair, narrates a long romance in the soft Suzhou dialect, chanting the sung passages to a three-stringed sanxian and a pipa. It is a blend of 评话 (pinghua, spoken tale) and 弹词 (tanci, sung tale), traced to the Ming-Qing period. Yanzhi's mother ran off with such a ballad-singer. Historical (corroborated).

The case is woven from the pared, dried stems of wisteria vine (紫藤), cheap and sturdy country luggage. It is Yanzhi's one constant possession, carried out of the shop and back into it across the years. (Material culture.)

ch42.note: The Shanghai Academy of Fine Arts (上海美术专科学校, 上海美专), founded in 1912 by the young painter Liu Haisu in the French Concession, was the first modern art school in China. It was famous, and notorious, for its Western methods, co-education and life-drawing from nude models among them, for which Liu was denounced as an “artistic traitor” but defended by the educator Cai Yuanpei. Historical (corroborated).

The Sincere Company (先施公司), founded by the Australia-returned merchant Ma Ying-piu, opened its grand Nanjing Road store in 1917, one of the “Four Great Department Stores” of Shanghai and a temple of modern glamour, cosmetics counters and rooftop garden and all. That the two women chat of its lipsticks marks their shared Shanghai worldliness. Historical (corroborated).

ch42.anchor: Temple Road was as quiet as a virgin
ch42.note: Jing'an Temple Road (静安寺路), better known by its old foreign name Bubbling Well Road, was one of the great westward thoroughfares of Shanghai, running out past the Paramount toward the Jing'an Temple; today it is Nanjing West Road. Qin Shuji keeps Yanzhi in an apartment here. Historical.

The building is full of 姨太太 and 小老婆, concubines and “small wives,” women kept by well-off men in separate flats, as Miss Lin is kept. Yanzhi, unpaid and unmarried to Qin Shuji, is of their number, and refuses to be. (Social structure.)

Miss Lin throws the proverb 既当婊子又立牌坊, “to play the whore and raise a chastity arch too”: to sin and still claim virtue. A 牌坊 is a stone memorial arch, and the state once erected such arches to honor widows who kept their chastity. Yanzhi's refusal of money strikes Miss Lin as exactly this hypocrisy. (Idiom / custom.)

ch42.anchor: a seal of the Shanghai Garrison Command
ch42.note: The Garrison Command (警备司令部) was the military authority that policed the city; a seal pasted across a door meant the premises had been closed and its occupant detained or wanted. That both the gallery and Qin Shuji's room are sealed is the only sign the novella gives of what became of him. Historical (institution).

ch43.anchor: make our old master his grave-clothes
ch43.note: Grave-clothes (寿衣, literally “longevity clothes”) are the burial garments prepared for the dead, traditionally in an antique cut and odd number of layers; a good suit was often made ready in advance. To sew one for a man killed so that not a whole bone was left is the tailor's grim office here. (Material culture / custom.)

The peace-preservation association (维持会) was the stopgap local council the Japanese set up in each newly occupied town to keep order and gather supplies, staffed by whatever local notables would serve; its head, like Young Master Tang, was by definition a collaborator. The chamber of commerce (商会) was folded into the same administration. Historical.

ch43.anchor: taking the thief for your father
ch43.note: The elder's phrase is the set idiom 认贼作父, “to acknowledge the thief as your father”: to serve, as kin, the enemy who has wronged your own. (Idiom.)

ch43.anchor: call me Mrs. Hu, or Shimu
ch43.note: Baosheng's surname is Hu; as his wife Yanzhi is 胡太太, Mrs. Hu. Shimu (师母, “teacher-mother”) is the title an apprentice gives his master's wife, Yanzhi's due now that Baosheng has inherited the shop and its craft. She corrects Young Master Tang's over-familiar use of her given name with it. (Honorific.)

ch43.anchor: Federal Reserve notes, tomorrow Central Reserve notes
ch43.note: Two of the occupation's puppet currencies. The Federal Reserve Bank of China (中国联合准备银行) issued its notes (联银券) from 1938 for the Japanese-sponsored regime in North China; the Central Reserve Bank (中央储备银行) issued the notes (中储券) of Wang Jingwei's regime in the lower Yangtze. Strictly the first belonged to the north; Yanzhi names the two together for the churn of worthless paper the occupation brought, both eaten alive by inflation. Historical (corroborated).

The Mid-Autumn Festival (中秋), the eighth-moon full-moon festival, a time of family reunion. A new shop would normally open on such a day with firecrackers and a feast; the Japanese ban on any bang that might be mistaken for gunfire forces Baosheng to open his cloth trade in silence. (Custom.)

ch44.note: Taijun (太君) was the deferential word occupied Chinese were made to use for a Japanese soldier or officer, roughly “His Honor, the master.” Its origin is disputed, perhaps a garbling of a Japanese form of address, but in wartime usage it reeked of servility to the invader. Historical.

ch44.anchor: getting a taste of the foreign
ch44.note: “To break the foreign fast” (开洋荤): to try some exotic, imported thing for the first time, here the tinned Japanese beef pressed on the very men about to be killed. (Idiom.)

A dalian (褡裢) is a long cloth carrying-bag, open at the middle and sewn shut at both ends, slung over the shoulder so a load hangs front and back: the pedlar's and the traveller's luggage. (Material culture.)

ch44.anchor: To lift the tea meant the guest was dismissed
ch44.note: “Lifting the tea” (端茶送客) was a genteel dismissal: when a host raised his own teacup, the caller understood the interview was over and rose to go. An old official courtesy, used here by a pawnbroker to be rid of a woman he will not help. Historical (custom).

ch44.anchor: rich water doesn't run into another man's field
ch44.note: The proverb 肥水不流外人田, “don't let your rich water drain into an outsider's field”: keep the good things, and the good matches, within the family or the circle. Yanzhi's father used it, Young Master Tang claims, to refuse him her hand. (Proverb.)

ch45.note: The bandits' word is 肉票, literally a “meat ticket”: a person held for ransom, the human counterpart of a pawn-ticket to be redeemed for silver. (Slang / custom.)

ch45.anchor: plucking a feather from every passing goose
ch45.note: The set phrase 雁过拔毛, “pluck a feather from every goose that flies over”: to take a cut from everything and everyone that passes. The bandits' rule that every ransomed woman be used is dressed in this cold proverb of universal extortion. (Idiom.)

Zhu Qi consults the 皇历 (or 黄历), the traditional almanac that marks each day as auspicious or ill-omened for particular undertakings; 宜嫁娶, “fit for marriage,” is one of its standing rubrics. Choosing a lucky day for a wedding was all but universal. (Custom.)
Bakayarō (八格牙路, from the Japanese ばか野郎): “idiot,” “damned fool,” a common Japanese curse transliterated into Chinese characters. (Japanese.)

ch45.anchor: the fowling-piece Old Mo handed him
ch45.note: A huochong (火铳) is an old muzzle-loading matchlock or hand-gun, the crude firearm of country bandits, no match, as the chapter shows, for the Japanese soldiers' bolt-action rifles. (Material culture.)
Zhu Qi reaches for the idiom 双喜临门, “a double happiness at the gate”: two joys at once, here his coming wedding and the captured steam-launch. The irony is the author's. (Idiom.)

ch46.note: “Pockmarked Liu” renders 刘麻子: the surname Liu with the by-name 麻子, “pockmarks,” the pitted scars left by smallpox. Such a nickname, fixing a man by a bodily defect, is common and unsentimental. (Telling name.)

The objection invokes 兄弟相煎, “brothers boiling one another,” from the poet Cao Zhi (192–232) and his “Poem of Seven Steps”: beans weeping in the pot as they cook over a fire of their own bean-stalks, “we sprang from the same root; why so fierce to burn each other?” To fall on a sworn brother's people breaks that bond. Historical (the poem is corroborated; the seven-paces legend is traditional).

The “rule handed down” is the levirate: on a man's death his widow, and here his whole following, pass to a brother, real or sworn, who inherits them along with his goods. The custom (转房婚 or 收继婚) is attested for centuries among Han Chinese as well as many other peoples; the word 大嫂, “elder brother's wife,” below carries the same logic. Historical (corroborated).

Big Sister-in-law (大嫂) is literally “eldest brother's wife.” Among the bandits, as the next lines explain, it is not mere address but a rank, the chief's woman who now holds the chief's authority, 当家的, “the one who runs the house.” Yanzhi has made herself their head. (Honorific / social structure.)

ch47.note: 忠义, “loyalty and honor” (or loyalty and righteousness), is the cardinal virtue of the Chinese outlaw-brotherhood tradition, enshrined in the classic novel 水溹传 (Water Margin), whose bandit heroes muster beneath a Hall of Loyalty and Righteousness (忠义堂). To set a spirit-tablet (牌位) bearing these words at the prow makes the boat a temple to the code; the water bandits swear by it. (Cultural.)

ch47.anchor: Boss, why put yourself through this
ch47.note: The men's word is 当家的, “the one who runs the house” — the office named at the close of the previous installment, now their way of addressing Yanzhi, and rendered “Boss” throughout. That a woman should be the 当家的 of a bandit band inverts the word's domestic root, the wife who manages a household. (Address form.)

ch47.anchor: past sixty and long a student of the Buddha
ch47.note: 年过花甲, “past the flowering 遴遴.” A 花甲 (huajia) is one full turn of the sexagenary cycle, the sixty-year round made by pairing the ten Heavenly Stems with the twelve Earthly Branches; to have passed it is to be over sixty. (Idiom; historical, corroborated.)

ch47.anchor: a wrong carried over from a former life
ch47.note: The doctor frames the child's deafness as 前世的冤宾 — a 冤宾 (karmic debt of sin and suffering) owed from a former existence — and urges Yanzhi instead to 烧香积德, to burn incense and lay up merit (功德), the good works that Buddhist belief holds can offset such a debt. The verdict is the folk-Buddhist commonplace that a congenital affliction is retribution for a past life. (Belief.)

ch47.anchor: three gold bars for a travel pass
ch47.note: A 路条 (lutiao) was the travel permit the occupation authorities required for movement between towns; without one a traveler could be turned back or seized at any checkpoint. That a single pass cost three gold bars measures both the blockade's grip and Yanzhi's desperation. (Institutions; historical.)

ch47.anchor: Next month is your father's death-day
ch47.note: A 忌辰 (jichen), the anniversary of a parent's death, is kept with offerings at the family altar or the grave; observing it is a core act of filial duty. Baosheng invokes it to bind Yanzhi to the household, and her answer — that he may count her dead as well — refuses both the duty and the marriage. (Custom.)

ch48.anchor: waiting for you all at the Fenshui Pavilion
ch48.note: 分水亭, literally the “dividing-the-waters pavilion,” a pavilion set where a channel forks. The name shadows the scene: it is where Qin Shuji tells Yanzhi to wait for him, and where, in the end, their lives part. Rendered “the Fenshui Pavilion.” (Place; the play on parting is the author's.)

ch48.anchor: spend a night at the Xingchun Lou
ch48.note: 杏春楼, the “Apricot-Spring House,” a brothel in the county town. The word 春 (“spring”) in such a name signals a pleasure-house, and Old Mo names it among the comforts the disciplined New Fourth Army could never grant his men. Rendered “the Xingchun Lou.” (Material culture.)

ch48.anchor: a hundred li away in the Tianmu Mountains
ch48.note: 天目山, the Tianmu range of northwest Zhejiang, a rugged massif that the New Fourth Army's Suzhou-Zhejiang Military District opened as a base area early in 1945; the Japanese mounted repeated mopping-up sweeps (户荡) against such base areas. (Geography; historical, corroborated.)

ch48.anchor: Yanzhi agreed to rise with them three days on
ch48.note: The word is 举义, “to raise a righteous rising” — to take up arms for a just cause, or to bring an armed band over to it. Here it means leading her bandits out of banditry and into the New Fourth Army. (Loaded term.)

ch49.anchor: victory in the War of Resistance
ch49.note: The War of Resistance against Japan (抗日战争, 1937–1945) ended with Japan's surrender in August 1945. Word of it reaches this backwater late and stirs the villagers little; the peace will be brief, for civil war follows within the year. (Historical, corroborated.)

ch49.anchor: a live-in son-in-law for the girl
ch49.note: 招上门女岳 — to bring in a son-in-law who marries into the wife's family, lives under her roof, and whose children may take her surname. A recourse for a family with a daughter and no son, it reversed the usual patrilocal marriage and carried a faint stigma for the man. Yanzhi plans it so that her deaf-mute daughter need never leave home. (Custom.)

With the peace came the reckoning with the 汉奧, the collaborators. Young Master Tang, who had served the occupation as headman, and the town's other notables are executed for collaboration (汉奧罪), for narcotics (the occupation economy ran on the opium trade), and for trafficking. Such trials and executions of collaborators were carried out across the recovered territories after 1945. (Historical, corroborated.)

ch49.anchor: five mu of land in the village besides, and a water buffalo
ch49.note: A 亩 (mu) is the standard Chinese unit of land area, about one-fifteenth of a hectare (some 667 square meters); five mu is a modest smallholding, enough for a family to work. (Measure.)

ch49.anchor: an American-style uniform and carried a revolver
ch49.note: The young officer's American uniform and his men's carbines mark them as one of the Nationalist units armed and re-equipped by the United States during and after the war; such matériel flooded the Nationalist forces in the civil war of 1946–1949. (Historical, corroborated.)

ch49.anchor: reorganized into a single Type-B company
ch49.note: The Nationalist army graded its formations 甲种 and 乙种, “Type A” and “Type B,” the latter under-strength and lightly armed. To fold the bandits into a Type-B company and march them to the Yangtze front was, as Scarface Qiang says, to make cannon-fodder of them. (Institutions; military.)

ch49.anchor: in a clash with the People's Liberation Army
ch49.note: The People's Liberation Army (人民解放军) was the Communist army that defeated the Nationalists in the civil war of 1946–1949 and founded the People's Republic that October; its several field armies are named elsewhere in this book. (Historical.)

ch49.anchor: work team taken up quarters in the village
ch49.note: A 工作组 (“work team”) was a squad of Party cadres sent into a newly liberated village to take charge of it — registering the people, redistributing land, and singling out “enemies of the people.” It is such a team that occupies Yanzhi's courtyard and to which she is denounced. (Institutions.)

ch49.anchor: the Military Affairs Commission of the People's Liberation Army
ch49.note: The source calls the occupying office a 军委会 (Military Affairs Commission). At the takeover of a town the Communists in fact set up a 军事管制委员会, a military-control committee, to govern it in the interim; the source's looser wording is rendered as it stands. (Institutions; the term is the source's.)

ch50.note: 取若木鸡, “dumb as a wooden chicken” — frozen, stupefied, unable to stir. The image comes from a parable in the Zhuangzi (《庄子·达生》): a fighting cock trained to such composure that it stands motionless as if carved of wood, and cows every rival into flight. The classical praise has since curdled into a byword for dull stupefaction. (Idiom; allusion.)

ch50.anchor: the wife of Comrade Qin Shuji
ch50.note: 同志, “comrade,” is the fellow-member address of the Party; 爱人, literally “loved one,” is the word the new society used for a spouse of either sex, in place of the old 太太 (“Mrs.”) that Yanzhi still reaches for. The change of vocabulary marks the change of worlds. (Loaded keywords.)

ch50.anchor: fallen in the fighting to liberate southern Zhejiang
ch50.note: The word for Qin Shuji's death is 牺牛, “to be sacrificed” — the term reserved for those who die for the revolutionary cause, marking him a martyr and not a mere casualty. 解放浙南, “the liberation of southern Zhejiang,” refers to the Communist campaigns that took the region in 1949. (Loaded keyword; historical.)

组织, “the organization,” is the Party spoken of as an entity owed absolute candor and obedience; to have deceived it for a private attachment is, in Yang Shuqin's eyes, Qin Shuji's true transgression, and the ground of her verdict on Yanzhi. (Loaded keyword.)

ch50.anchor: the black mourning-band bound about her left arm
ch50.note: A band of black cloth (黑纱) worn on the left upper arm is the customary sign of mourning for a close kin or comrade; it is this band that tells Yanzhi, before the words do, that Qin Shuji is dead. (Custom.)

ch51.note: “New China” (新中国) is the People's Republic, proclaimed in Beijing on 1 October 1949; “the first spring festival since the founding of New China” sets the book's close in the opening weeks of 1950, at the new state's first lunar New Year. (Historical, corroborated.)

ch51.anchor: five mu of land had long since been parceled out to two households
ch51.note: Under land reform (土地改革, 土改), the redistributive campaign that came with the Communist takeover of the countryside, the holdings of landlords and the well-to-do were confiscated and parceled out to poor and landless peasants. Yanzhi's five mu, bought with a bandit's spoils, have been split between two households and her courtyard turned to public use. (Historical, corroborated.)

ch51.anchor: the world of the laboring people
ch51.note: 劳动人民的天下, “the realm belongs to the laboring people now” — a stock phrase of the new order, declaring that power and property have passed to the workers and peasants. In the team head's mouth it is the courteous refusal of Yanzhi's claim on her own house. (Loaded slogan.)

ch51.anchor: a bourgeois thing like that had long since been buried along with the old society
ch51.note: 资产阶级, “bourgeois,” and 旧社会, “the old society,” are the new regime's terms for the propertied class and the pre-1949 order it displaced. Qin Shuji's portrait of Yanzhi — the one thing she came back for — is condemned under the first name and consigned to the second. (Loaded keywords.)
